title: Families v loyal fans - women's football's attendance dilemma

Average Women's Super League attendances surged by 192% in the season after the Lionesses' Euro 2022 triumph, but the speed of the boom has stalled.
Median crowds have risen by just 166 fans, from 3,070 in 2023-24 to 3,236 in 2025-2026, according to a 2026 report from YouGov and architecture firm Populous, external.
Some of the biggest fixtures are now attracting significantly smaller attendances.
Arsenal against Manchester United at Emirates Stadium fell from 46,603 in 2024-25 to 29,853 this season, while Chelsea v Arsenal dropped from 34,302 to 19,349 over the same period.

The Gunners, who averaged 34,000 at the Emirates last season - almost four times the next-highest club, Chelsea, and higher than eight Premier League sides, external - had just 19,546 for their October match against Birmingham City.
There are bright spots, including a sold-out 4,000-ticket Arsenal away allocation at Tottenham for the first time, but the wider trend for some matches is clear.
Manchester United against Manchester City was hosted at Leigh Village in October with a crowd of 5,361. The same fixture was held at Old Trafford in March 2026 with 24,983 fans.
So what is behind the decline? Marketing, scheduling, matchday experience, stadium design, product or something else?

When supporters were asked what mattered most to their enjoyment of a women's football match in the report, a "welcoming, family-friendly environment" ranked above team success and the quality of on-pitch performance for both established and potential fans.
The research found only 15% of fans who have attended a women's match in the past five years do so at least monthly.
Meanwhile, 43% describe themselves as casual followers who engage more with major international tournaments than domestic club football, while just 10% identify as devoted supporters.
The findings suggest there is a possible matchday "experience gap" in the domestic game, with some clubs seeking to address it through family-friendly initiatives.
However, some fans have voiced their frustration at the family-friendly marketing.
Tottenham fan Dakota said "I'm almost glad I can't make it" in relation to a Spurs social media advert about the north London derby, which listed DJs, drinks, face painting and freestylers.
Image source, Tottenham HotspurShe added: "We'll never grow as a women's club if the entire marketing is for kids and families rather than young adults with disposable income."
Spurs fan Rosewen had similar views: "They can offer attractions to tempt people through the gates but we're losing sight of football and the importance of winning."

On the recent low crowd for the north London derby, one fan wrote on X: "Attendances across the WSL are down so this isn't a Spurs specific issue. However, the club has used a one-dimensional family-friendly marketing strategy for years."

Brighton took a similar family-focused approach for their October match against West Ham at the Amex, promoting a "Saturday Spooktacular" with attractions including a haunted house, face-painting, hair braiding, costume competitions and other activities taking up the majority of the advert.

Image source, Brighton and Hove AlbionHow does scheduling impact crowd numbers? Premier League football has long owned the 3pm Saturday slot while the WSL has varied kick-off times, making it harder for fans to establish a regular routine.
